🗒️What This Means For You
  • Stocks: Stocks fell across the board; small companies dropped the most, nearly 1.8%.
  • FX: The dollar barely moved tonight; the euro is still weaker than its recent averages.
  • Technicals: Stocks are still well above their long-run averages, a very stretched position historically.
  • Sectors: Only energy rose; utilities, property and media sank as borrowing costs jumped.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lenders still charge companies almost the lowest extra interest ever, which leaves little cushion.
  • Crisis: Overall stress looks moderate, but Iran oil risk and government debt worries are rising.
  • Inflation: Core inflation is steady but not falling fast, and energy prices keep it sticky.
  • Tech Bubble: Chip stocks are near dot-com froth, but the broader market is far less extreme.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Micron reports September 30 and options price a big move; the US IPO calendar could not be confirmed.
  • Iran: Trump met Iran's foreign minister and says a deal-or-escalate decision is coming.
  • Warsh: Warsh raised rates in September and sounds ready to raise them again.
  • Week Ahead: Next week: consumer confidence, job openings, GDP and the Fed's preferred inflation measure.
  • Outlook: Near-term cautious: rising bond yields and Iran headlines outweigh strong tech earnings.
  • Trades: Favor energy as a hedge, cut junk bonds, and avoid small caps while yields climb.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 buy, 2 sell, 24 hold long, 18 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.86 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 100th pctile, -0bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle; short term: 3y cup (2023-2026) complete, 109% retracement, pass level 4.85%.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Bond yields are driving markets now, so be careful and keep hedges on.

The day's biggest story was a sharp bond selloff. The US 10Y rose 0.1529 to 5.1142% and the 2Y rose 0.1438 to 4.8973%. Bund (3.555%, +0.092) and Gilt (5.347%, +0.109) yields rose with them. Equities fell as a result: the S&P 500 lost 0.75% to 7706.03, the Nasdaq Composite fell 1.13% to 26936.04, the Dow fell 0.68%, and the Russell 2000 fell 1.77% to 2838.66. VIX rose 0.97 to 15.18. Compared with the prior session, this was a clear risk-off turn. Only Energy (+1.04%) rose, with Brent at 103.08. Rate-sensitive Utilities (-1.87%), Real Estate (-1.49%) and Comm Services (-1.89%) led the losses. The macro backdrop is a hawkish Warsh Fed, which raised rates to 3.75–4.00% on September 16, plus a live US–Iran standoff over the Strait of Hormuz. Trump met Iran's foreign minister Araghchi at the UN and called it a 'very good meeting', but also said he has a 'big decision' between a deal and escalation. Mood is cautious but not panicked. Credit barely moved: US IG OAS rose 0.01 to 0.76 and HY OAS rose 0.08 to 2.74, and both remain near historic tights.

📊Markets

US equities closed lower across the board. S&P 500 7706.03 (-0.75%, -58.61), Nasdaq Composite 26936.04 (-1.13%, -308.24), Dow 51511.59 (-0.68%, -352.10), Russell 2000 2838.66 (-1.77%). Small caps did worst, as expected when yields jump, because they depend more on floating-rate borrowing. VIX rose to 15.18 from 14.21, which is still a low-volatility regime. Global yields followed: Bund 10Y 3.555%, Gilt 10Y 5.347%, and JGB 10Y unchanged at 2.989%. In commodities, WTI was 92.10 (-0.07% live), Brent was 103.08 (+3.86% as reported), gold 4286.86, silver 64.358 and copper 667.80 (-1.21%).

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.86 vol points (68th percentile of the 25 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 95.5 (69th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 98bp (steeper by 35bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 73% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (105bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.11 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 73%.

No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

On the computed analog chart, the current Nasdaq path is at month 47 from the Oct-2022 anchor at 245.1. The dot-com path from Oct-1990 was 231.7 at month 47 and did not peak until month 113. So today's run tracks the 1990s trajectory closely but is roughly mid-cycle on that template, not at its blow-off. The valuation marker sits at 22% of the 2000 peak P/E. The bubble risk is less about headline multiples and more about where the froth sits. First, semiconductors: SOX P/E is near the 2000 extreme, and Micron is expected to report roughly 10x year-on-year EPS on September 30. Second, credit and volatility complacency, with IG/Baa spreads and VIX beyond 2000-peak tightness. The catalyst that ended 2000 was Fed tightening into a flattening curve. Today Warsh is hiking (3.75–4.00%), the 10Y is at 5.1142%, and the 2s10s is still positive at 21.69bp. The ingredients are forming but the curve has not signalled yet. The five inputs above (top-10 concentration, IPO froth, CAPE, Buffett ratio, long-term EPS growth expectations) are analyst estimates from general knowledge. They were not verified by web search this run and should be treated as approximate.

Reports fiscal Q4 on Sep 30 after the close. Consensus is about $31.16 EPS vs $3.03 a year ago, on revenue near $50.4bn vs $11.32bn. Bloomberg implied vol is 61.0481, the highest in the candidate set, so the options market expects a large move either way.

The focus is whether memory pricing power lasts. HBM supply for 2026 is reported fully booked, HBM4 is shipping for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform, and DRAM spot prices are reportedly up 52% since January. The stock is up about 240% in 2026 and trades around 6x forward earnings (Benzinga, Motley Fool). With the SOX at 93% of 2000-peak P/E conditions, MU is the bellwether test of the semis froth.

⚔️Iran War

Diplomacy and escalation threats are running side by side. On September 23, Trump met Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, for about three hours on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly and called it a 'very good meeting' (Al Jazeera, CBS). Iranian state TV said the US requested the meeting and that it was about conveying Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Iran confirmed US contact via Qatar in New York (The National). At the UN, Trump said he has a 'big decision' on whether to make a deal or drive Iran 'into hell' (CBS). President Pezeshkian said Iran is ready for dialogue but not 'the language of force'. Sanctions are tightening: Treasury Secretary Bessent said all Iranian airlines would be shut down globally from September 23, with service providers cut off from the dollar system, and Iraq said it would enforce the ban from September 22. Secretary of State Rubio said military options remain available. GlobalSecurity marks September 22 as Day 207 of the war. For markets: Brent at 103.08 and Energy's +1.04% show the Hormuz premium is intact. A deal is the main downside risk for oil; escalation is the main tail risk for everything else.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Most likely: another 25bp hike or a hawkish hold with an explicit tightening bias at the next FOMC. Analyst estimate: 55% hike / 45% hold. That is inference from his on-record stance: the September 16 hike to 3.75–4.00%, his repeated 'work to do' and 'deliver price stability' language, and a Jackson Hole speech that analysts read as raising hike odds. A Hormuz-driven growth or market shock would push him toward a hold.

~1 YEAR

Inference: a policy rate held at or modestly above today's 3.75–4.00% range, with a continued smaller and shorter-duration balance sheet. He has long favored shrinking the Fed's holdings, and he says short-term rates should stay the main policy tool. Expect institutional changes from his five task forces (Communications, Balance Sheet, Data Sources, Productivity and Jobs, Inflation Framework), with recommendations due by year-end. That could mean less forward guidance and a possible reframing of the inflation target. Cuts within a year would need Core PCE (now 3.34415%) to fall clearly toward the trimmed-mean readings.

Warsh became chair on May 13, 2026. He held in July and hiked 25bp on September 16. At Jackson Hole he sounded hawkish enough that CNBC's analyst roundup said hike odds rose and the Fed may be 'at odds' with Treasury. His record combines inflation-first rhetoric, dislike of large balance sheets and skepticism of forward guidance. So the market should expect less hand-holding and more data dependence, which is consistent with today's jump in 2Y and 10Y yields. The risk is a Fed–Treasury clash if long yields above 5% start to strain deficit financing. The one-year view above is inference from his statements, not a stated plan.

Sources: September 16, 2026 Chairman Warsh's Press Conference (Federal Reserve) · Jackson Hole analyst roundup: Warsh's speech sends hike chances higher (CNBC) · Kevin Warsh Says There's Still 'Work to Do' to Fight Inflation (Chase) · Fed Outlook 2026: Rate forecasts and fixed income strategies (iShares) · Warsh dilemma (Allianz Trade)
